Chapter 8: The Power of Example
As the years on the job added up, something interesting happened. The role of being a mentor—of leading by example—became more and more important.
People starting out in their careers—young officers, new staff, even civilians—would look to those in charge for cues. They watched how you acted, how you led, and especially, how you handled the tough moments. That’s a responsibility you just can’t shrug off.
I remember a day when a junior officer, clearly nervous and unsure, came to me for advice. The conversation was short, but what stuck with me was how much those little things—a kind word, honest feedback, or just taking the time to listen—could truly shape someone’s path.
Most folks don’t realize just how powerful a good example can be. But if you've ever had a mentor who made a difference, you know how quietly strong that influence really is.
Now, out in public, there’s always that pull to put on a show, to play to the crowd. But real leadership? That happens far from the cameras. It’s in the choices you make each day, the private chats, and the moments when you’re willing to own up to mistakes.
I’ve had times when a public slip-up brought on criticism and doubt. But those moments? They’re also a chance to show what accountability really looks like. And here’s something to remember: people won’t just recall what you accomplished—they’ll remember how you acted when things got tough.
This power of example isn’t just for the military. It’s true in communities, in schools, and at home. Integrity, respect, service—these aren’t just things you talk about. They’re habits, built day by day, tested when life gets rough, and passed on by what you do, not just what you say.
When I look back, what really matters isn’t the titles or awards. It’s seeing the people you’ve mentored go on to do great things. There’s a quiet pride in knowing that something you said, or did, made a real difference.
That’s the true reward of a life spent in service.
